Earth's rotation speed at the equator is about 1,670 km/h (the book's 1,180 km/h is roughly the speed at mid-latitudes); orbital speed of about 107,000 km/h is correct. Recorded as printed.

decorative: Illustration of a stepped waterfall with pink lotus flowers in the foreground, representing a river of Paradise.
issues: Hadith sources describe the water as whiter than milk, sweeter than honey and (in some narrations) colder than snow; references are not given in the book.
The hadith "Allah does not look at your forms and wealth but at your hearts and deeds" is in Sahih Muslim (2564); the book gives no reference.

decorative: Photograph of pilgrims in white ihram performing tawaf around the Ka'bah.
issues: The lesson text does not explicitly state the "good news" asked in 2(ہ); the answer is inferred from the lesson.
The question calls Surah Al-Muddaththir the "second revelation", while the lesson text does not say so; it is commonly described as among the earliest revelations after Surah Al-Alaq.

Only the Urdu translation of this hadith is printed (no Arabic text). The reference "Musnad Ahmad: 1012" could not be verified here (the narration from Abu Dharr is usually numbered 21556 in Musnad Ahmad); flagged for review.
This hadith is usually cited as Sahih Bukhari 645; the reference "219" is recorded as printed.
Schools of fiqh count the conditions and pillars of prayer differently; the 7 + 6 = 13 division follows the Hanafi presentation common in Pakistani textbooks.

decorative: Photograph of worshippers praying in rows around the Ka'bah in Masjid al-Haram.
issues: Most schools of fiqh count reciting Surah Al-Fatihah itself as part of the obligatory recitation; the book's definition follows the Hanafi wording. Recorded as printed.
The number "6" before "قعدہ کرنا" is missing in the printed book. Recorded with the number added.

The welcome song is printed in Arabic only; the meaning given is this edition's rendering, flagged for review. Historians note that the song is reported in later sources (e.g. Bayhaqi) and its exact occasion is debated.
Sources usually state that 45 Muhajirin were paired with 45 Ansar (90 men in all) at the first Mu'akhat; the book mentions only the 45 Muhajirin. Recorded as printed.
The inheritance between Muhajirin and Ansar brothers was later abrogated by Surah Al-Anfal 8:75 (inheritance returned to blood relatives). Recorded as printed.
This paragraph describes "the Jews" of Madinah collectively; historians attribute these roles to particular tribes and individuals. Recorded as printed.

decorative: Painting of a country road leading through golden fields towards a sunrise, with a few trees on the horizon.
issues: The Muslims also faced Bait-ul-Maqdis for the 16–17 months in Madinah; the change came in Madinah, as the text goes on to say.
The inset map in the book marks the Madinah–Badr distance as about 150 km, while the text says about 158 km. Recorded as printed.
The claim that Badr is "the only battle" in which angels took part is a common view, but some reports mention angels at other battles (e.g. Hunayn, 9:26). Recorded as printed.
The story of Ukkashah's wooden sword is reported in the Seerah of Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham rather than in the major hadith collections. Recorded as printed.

The lesson text does not say which Muslim killed which opponent; the usual account (Ali vs. Walid, Hamzah vs. Shaibah, Ubaidah vs. Utbah) is followed. The book's map pairs Ali with Walid, consistent with this.
Printed page 51 ends "…مدینہ منورہ پر حملہ آور ہونے پر قائل" and page 52 begins with a new heading, so the end of the sentence ("کر لیا" — "persuaded them") is missing in the book.
Seerah sources usually give the Makkan cavalry as 200 horses and 700 armoured men; the book's "100 skilled archers" is recorded as printed.

Calling the Makkans "defeated" is the book's interpretation; historians generally describe Uhud as a tactical setback for the Muslims, with the Quraish withdrawing without pressing on to Madinah (the pursuit to Hamra' al-Asad). Recorded as printed.
Wahshi later accepted Islam; the book does not mention this.
Point (5) on consultation is drawn from the lesson's narrative and learning outcomes, not from the printed list of results.
This famous reply is often attributed to Hazrat Zaid bin Dathinah, who was captured with Hazrat Khubaib; some Seerah sources link it to Khubaib. Recorded as printed.
Scan 066 is a duplicate of scan 064 (printed page 58); not repeated here.
Scan 067 is a duplicate of scan 065 (printed page 59); not repeated here.
This narration is usually reported from Abdullah bin Buraidah from his father Buraidah (Sunan Abi Dawud 1109, Tirmidhi 3774). Recorded as printed.
The phrase "يَا اَبَا عُمَيْرٍ مَا فَعَلَ النُّغَيْرُ" is printed in Arabic; its translation is given in the book. The reference Tirmidhi 333 is recorded as printed (commonly cited as Bukhari 6129).
In the hadith the Prophet ﷺ says he does not break covenants nor detain envoys. The envoy (Abu Rafi') later returned and became Muslim. Recorded as printed.
The two men in this hadith are Hazrat Hudhayfah bin al-Yaman and his father. Recorded as printed.
Scholars differ on whether consultation is obligatory (wajib) or recommended for individuals; the book's statement is recorded as printed.
The Muslim army reached Tabuk, but the Byzantine army did not come to meet it; "reaching the Roman army" is the book's wording. Recorded as printed.
Options (a) and (b) are both supported by the lesson (the hadith and the proverb); the answer follows the hadith named in the question.

The claim that patience was "the first" moral quality urged on the Prophet ﷺ reflects early revelations such as Al-Muddaththir 74:7 ("وَلِرَبِّكَ فَاصْبِرْ"); Al-Ahqaf 46:35 is a later Makkan verse. Recorded as printed.

issues: Options (a) and (d) are both correct according to the lesson, which says controlling emotions is called both sabr and tahammul.

issues: The book says the Prophet ﷺ declared the dishonest person "ایمان سے خارج"; the hadith that follows denies (complete) faith (نفیِ کمال). The English adds "(the perfection of)" for clarity; the Urdu is kept exactly as printed.

The verse is quoted only in part, as in the book (Al-Ma'idah 5:38 continues "نَكَالًا مِّنَ اللّٰهِ ۭ وَاللّٰهُ عَزِيْزٌ حَكِيْمٌ"). The Arabic diacritics follow the standard mushaf and were checked against the scan. Flag for review.

issues: The book's translation says "اللہ سے ڈرتے ہیں" for وَيَخْشَوْنَ رَبَّهُمْ ("fear their Lord"); the meaning is the same. The verse is quoted only in part. Arabic checked against the scan; flag for review.

decorative: Illustration of a red-earth path between grey rocks and green grass tufts.
issues: The book prints "حضرت زید بن ثابت". The freed slave whom the Prophet ﷺ raised and whose children he cherished was Zaid ibn Harithah (زید بن حارثہ), not the scribe Zaid ibn Thabit. This is likely a misprint. The Urdu is kept as printed; the English and Pashto say only "Zaid". Flag for review.

Research list: An-Nisa 4:85 is about intercession (شفاعت) rather than justice directly; the answer links it to justice by way of "good intercession = supporting what is right". The verse texts are not reproduced here; students are told to copy them from the mushaf. Flag for teacher review.

The book places Hazrat Usman's purchase of the well (Bi'r Rumah) in "this period", right after describing the period of prophethood in general. The purchase actually took place in Madinah after the Hijrah. The text is kept as printed.
Age at death: the book gives 64 years 6 months. Most biographies give about 65 lunar years (she was 40 at marriage, and the marriage lasted about 25 years). Kept as printed.
Sawdah's year of death is disputed in the sources: the end of Umar's caliphate (22/23 AH) or 54 AH. The book's 22 AH is kept.

decorative: Photograph of the Holy Ka'bah in Masjid al-Haram with worshippers in concentric rows of prayer.

issues: Chart: the tribe for Khadijah and Aishah is given as "Quraish" from general knowledge (Banu Asad and Banu Taym respectively); the lesson names only Sawdah's family. The lesson gives no ages for Sawdah or Aishah, so the age column is left out.

The lesson says three sons. The previous lesson (printed 104) says Khadijah bore "two sons"; together with Ibrahim (from Mariyah) that makes three. This is consistent. Abdullah's death "in Ta'if according to some narrations" is unusual (most sources say Makkah); kept as printed.

Clue row 1 ("faced difficulties and hardships") echoes the "Do you know?" box, which is about Zainab. The other clues (third daughter, died 9 AH) point clearly to Umm Kulthum, so that is the answer given.

The opening words "فَاطِمَةُ بَضْعَةٌ مِّنِّيْ فَمَنْ" and the start of the Urdu translation were supplied from the standard text of Bukhari 3714, which matches the cited number. Check against a clean copy of the book before publication.

issues: The learning outcomes (printed 113) mention the marriage of Fatimah and Ali and the Tasbihat of Fatimah, but the lesson text on printed 113–114 covers neither. Kept as printed; teachers may need to supply this material.
The activity labels (عملی کام، تقریری مقابلہ، ذہنی آزمائش) are faded on the scan; they were read from their outlines and the usual pattern of this book.
Zubair's age at death: the book says 67; many sources give 64 or 66–67. Kept as printed.
The book prints the father's name as "زید بن عمر بن نفیل"; the usual form is "زید بن عمرو بن نفیل" (عمرو with و). Written here with و, which is how the name is normally spelled.

The previous scan is printed 119; printed pages 120–121 are missing from every source (see p127). The answers below marked "متن دستیاب نہیں" come from standard sirah sources, not the missing text.
The question prints "قبیلہ تمیم" while the lesson (printed 117) says Talhah was of the clan "تیم". The answer is Talhah either way; here it is written as "تیم".
"خراسان کے گورنر کے کاتب" while living in Basra: historically, Hasan Basri served as secretary to al-Rabi' ibn Ziyad, the governor of Khurasan, during campaigns. The text is kept as printed.

Chronology problem in the book: Abdullah Shah Ghazi is said to be born in 98 AH, yet also to have fought with Muhammad bin Qasim against Raja Dahir, whose campaign was in 92–95 AH (711–714 CE), before that birth date. His father Muhammad Nafs-e-Zakiyyah was himself born about 93 AH. Both statements are kept as printed; flagged for review.

decorative: Photograph of a mosque with domes and minarets lit up at dusk.
issues: Nahawand is in western Iran (Hamadan province), within the wider Kurdish/Lur region. The book's "کردستان کے شہر نہاوند" is kept as printed.
Abdullah Shah Ghazi's place of death: the lesson says only that the caliph's agents martyred him while the governor of Sindh was reluctant; "Sindh" is inferred from that. His shrine is in Karachi.
The teacher's name is printed "حماد بن سلیمان". He is usually called Hammad ibn Abi Sulaiman. Kept as printed.
"آپ نے صحابہ کرام سے علم حاصل کیا": Abu Hanifah met some Companions (e.g. Anas ibn Malik), which makes him a Tabi'i, but whether he studied hadith with them is debated. Kept as printed.
"علمِ حدیث پر لکھی جانے والی پہلی کتاب": al-Muwatta is among the earliest surviving compilations, but earlier written collections (sahifahs) existed. Kept as printed.

The book lists Ibn Shihab al-Zuhri among Imam Malik's students. Al-Zuhri (d. 124 AH) was in fact one of Malik's teachers; Awza'i and Thawri were his contemporaries, who narrated from him. Kept as printed; flagged for review.
The lesson does not state Imam Ja'far Sadiq's birthplace; "Madinah" is the standard view (and matches "most of his life in Madinah").

The research activity asks for the first hadith of al-Muwatta. Its Arabic text is not reproduced here, so that no Hadith text is added that the book itself does not print. Students are told to copy it from an authentic edition.

The book says Khalid never caused the Prophet ﷺ verbal or physical harm. Before accepting Islam, however, Khalid commanded the Quraish cavalry at Uhud. The statement probably refers to personal harm during the Makkan period. Kept as printed.
